new_statements.quote: Bhatise is on the east bank of the Indus opposite Besham. Instead of the pitch accent system of other varieties of Indus Kohistani, Bhatise has a complex system of interacting tones and stress accents.

new_statements.relation_note: One sentence, second-hand, in a handbook chapter by a Vedic specialist; the chapter's references contain no Bateri or Indus Kohistani source (Zoller cited only for 1988 Bangani; Baart 1997 for Kalam Kohistani), so the basis is unknown. It goes beyond, and partly against, the only primary source (Zoller 2005: 22-23: B lemmata carry rising/falling accent marks never checked instrumentally; B vowel system 'phonetically the most complicated'; B accent system expected to be 'quite similar' to Jijali pitch accent) and beyond Baart 2003 ('Bateri? Shina-type?'). The only published characterisation of Bateri as tone-plus-stress; cannot support a stress-placement reading.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Typological assertion only: Bateri is said NOT to share the two-way (rising vs falling) lexical pitch accent of the other Indus Kohistani varieties but to have tones and stress accents that interact. No stress position, no tone inventory, no forms, no source cited.
new_statements.identity_note: 'Bhatise is on the east bank of the Indus opposite Besham' = Zoller's Bhaṭīse/Baṭeṛa = Bateri (btv, bate1261); named as a fringe 'dialect' of Indus Kohistani (Maiya) beside Chiliso, Gabar (Gowro) and Kanyawali. | Bhaṭera = Batera village on the east bank of the Indus opposite the Karakorum Highway near Besham (Strand's intro on); Strand states that SIL later published 'their standard word list and a short text in Bhaṭʹe-sa zib.. by Hallberg (1992) under the misnomer "Bateri"' = the Bateri [btv] of Rensch/Hallberg 1992. new_statements.quote: Accent. There are two levels of accent, normal ʹ and strong ʹ . Accent is produced with an anterior tightening of the the vocal folds during vowel production, raising the pitch on the vowel. Pitch, vowel length, and tenseness apparently are a function of accent level. Unaccented vowels are low-pitched, lax, and short; accented vowels are higher-pitched, tenser, and longer, and strongly accented vowels are even higher-pitched and longer. The position of accent within words appears to be non-predictable.

(pp. 22-23) The lemmata from B and G have not been analyzed in this way. ... In case of the B words, many of the[m] have been marked either with the rising or the falling accent. This marking, however, was never checked with the speech analyzer. Nevertheless, all words collected in the two languages have been incorporated into this dictionary. It was not possible to analyze their accent systems with the speech analyzer, but each word was checked whether or not it had a parallel in Jijālī.' -- verbatim apart from the compiler ellipsis (omits the consultant names and 'work on these two language had to be put to the background') and extracted text diacritic rendering (Bhat.ı̄se). pp. 22-23 passage found at lines 1040-1051: 'The lemmata from B and G…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for bate1261, so there is nothing to agree or disagree with; this is the first primary-source statement. It supplies accent-marked Bateri lexical data and the author's expectation of a J-like (Shina-type) lexical pitch accent system, explicitly flagged as unanalysed. This is consistent with the second-hand note already logged in this language's Baart 2003 lists Bateri as tonal 'Yes?' and tentatively 'Shina-type?'). The work is primarily about Jijali Indus Kohistani (indu1241); only the B-tagged lemmata and the passages quoted concern Bateri.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bateri (B) words in the dictionary (~977 lemmata) are transcribed with a lexical accent, marked as rising (acute) or falling (grave) on one syllable per word, position varying by lexeme (e.g. áṅgo 'courtyard', aṅgùi 'finger', axòr 'hay', adràk 'ginger'); Zoller expects the B accent system to be 'quite similar' to the Jijali Indus Kohistani pitch accent system (two contrastive accents, rising vs falling; 'each morpheme contains one syllable either with a rising or a falling accent', p. 26; rising accent in the ultima shifts right onto a layer-I suffix). He states explicitly that the B accent system was NOT instrumentally analyzed and the rising/falling marking was never checked. Notational point (p. 23, p. 26 rule 1): in many B words the accent mark is written on the consonant preceding the tone-bearing vowel, because B has a shorter peak-delay than J and the early onset of the accent contour affects the preceding consonant. No rule predicting the place of the accent is given for B (nor for J: accent place is lexical).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for B. For J compounds Zoller marks a dominant 'nucleus' accent (n1/n2) with the other accent at a lower energy level (p. 28 rule 12); not stated for B.
new_statements.exceptions: B accent marking unverified ('never checked with the speech analyzer'); B vowel system described as phonetically the most complicated of the four varieties, allophony not yet incorporated (p. 22); B and G 'appear to have similar cases of accent shift under specific conditions' (p. 23) but the conditions are given only for J (pp. 26-28).
new_statements.identity_note: Zoller's 'Bhaṭīse (B) (also called Baṭera / Baṭērā in Pashto)', spoken on the east bank of the Indus opposite Besham (p. 1), consultant Akhtar Khan, is Bateri (bate1261, ISO btv). The volume as a whole describes the Jijālī (J) variety of Indus Kohistani (indu1241, Jijal village), with additional lemmata from Šāṭōṭī (Š), Seo (S), Gabār/Gowro (G, gowr1239) and Bhaṭīse (B); only the B-tagged material and the quoted passages bear on Bateri. The tag in the target record ('Gabār = Gowro') refers to a different language (Gowro), also covered in the same introduction.

Content = a 49-letter alphabet chart (Urdu letters plus څ ڇ ڙ ݜ), an aspirate-digraph page (بھ پھ تھ ٹھ جھ چھ ڇھ دھ ڈھ ڙھ کھ گھ), a vowel chart pairing short and long vowels (ا/آ، آٞ; اِ/ای; اےْ/اے; اُ/اُو; اوْ/او), and one picture-word page per letter (e.g. انگی 'finger', آنز 'fire', اِیڇ 'bear', نتھور 'nose').
